newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian lawyer says "British spy" mentally ill.
newsitem.headline: Russian lawyer says "British spy" mentally ill.

text.p: Russian judges met behind closed doors on Monday to decide whether a junior foreign ministry official alleged to have spied for Britain is mentally fit to stand trial, his attorney said.

The lawyer representing Platon Obukhov, 28, is hoping that criminal proceedings in a Moscow City Court could be dropped if the court decides he is unfit -- as his father, a former top diplomat, asserts.
"The court meeting was adjourned till tomorrow. So far our demand for a new (mental) checkup has been rejected," lawyer Anatoly Kucherena told Reuters.
"Tomorrow I will ask for it again. If it is rejected I will file a court claim within seven days."
He later told Ekho Moskvy radio that Obukhov was not in court for the hearing. He has been held since in April 1996 on charges he was paid for information by British MI6 agents.
A second secretary in the ministry's prestigious North America Department, Obukhov also wrote pulp spy thrillers on the side. His mother says he had trouble telling fact from fiction.
Obukhov's lawyer and his parents insist he has been mentally unstable since childhood and is unfit to stand trial. They want him discharged to a psychiatric hospital.

"If you analyse his whole life and all his deeds it will be evident that he is sick -- he has had schizophrenia... since he was about four years of age," said Alexander Gimervert, a psychiatrist for the defence.
However, the Federal Security Service (FSB) insists that Obukhov was quite sane while he was spying and that his illness cannot and should not free him from facing the court.
If the court rules Obukhov was sane at the time of the alleged crime and is capable in principle of facing charges, he will be admitted to hospital and tried when he recovers.
Psychiatric tests in 1996 and 1997 confirmed Obukhov was ill but did not rule out that he had been sane while spying.
Obukhov, son of a former Soviet deputy foreign minister and top arms negotiator, admitted spying for the British.
He was shown, wearing unmatched socks, admitting the charges in a television interview. "Before and after each contact I vomited. I could not eat. I was in panicky fear," he said.
It was not clear how much classified information he had access to. His father, recalled after his son's arrest from his post as ambassador to Denmark, insists he had no access at all.
Yet some of the Russian media, playing up the FSB's catch, compared Obukhov to the "giants of espionage", saying he had been in personal contact with senior British agents in Moscow.
Soon after Obukhov's arrest, several diplomats at the British embassy in Moscow were expelled, accused of links to a Russian citizen who had access to classified information.
In a Cold War-style tit-for-tat response, Britain expelled some Russian embassy officials.
The FSB says it caught 27 professional foreign spies last year and 60 Russians in the pay of foreign powers.
The head of the FSB said recently that foreign spy services were very active in Russia and he was shocked by how cheaply many Russians were prepared to sell out their country.
Those charged with treason before this year face the death sentence. New offenders face a maximum of 20 years in prison.
Two Russians, charged in previous years, were sentenced in the past month to terms of 10 and seven years hard labour, one for spying for the United States, the other for Britain.
